dimensions.assessment_basis: The preserved sources establish the bounded consequence described in the Incident summary: Stephens County Associate District Judge Lawrence Wheeler acknowledged using ChatGPT for legal research in connection with a 2025 child-paternity case order that contained citations to two cases that do not exist, according to an August 17, 2026 letter from District Attorney Jason Hicks describing Wheeler's statement to the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation. Reporting identifies the nonexistent cases as Cummings v. Cimarron Elevator Co. and Hawkins v. Linhart. Wheeler said he created the order himself and used ChatGPT only for research. The order was later vacated after an attorney challenged the citations at the Oklahoma Supreme Court. The Oklahoma Attorney General's Office stated that the evidence reviewed did not support criminal prosecution; possible judicial discipline remained a separate matter. Unreported downstream consequences were not inferred. Threshold applied: Meaningful but bounded denial, detention, exclusion or procedural deprivation that is substantially reversible.

public_interpretation_before: The material governance issue is epistemic reliance in an authoritative judicial artefact. Fictitious AI-produced case citations entered a signed court order even though the validity of judicial legal reasoning depends on materially higher source and authority fidelity than exploratory legal research. The reviewed evidence does not establish that Wheeler delegated authorship of the order to ChatGPT, and it does not expressly establish that a distinct required verification step was wholly omitted; VIGIL therefore does not infer Required Verification Omission as a secondary class. Fictitious-source and reliance-assurance failures are retained; the reported research use does not prove delegated authorship or complete omission of a distinct verification step. Vacatur and absence of criminal prosecution do not settle possible discipline. The safe-functioning outcome is Not aligned. The later occurrence review is Aligned for the examined material. Relevant assurance-documentation assessments remain Boundary where their decisive records are not available.

factual_basis_before: Reuters reports, based on an August 17, 2026 letter from Stephens County District Attorney Jason Hicks to the Oklahoma attorney general's office, that Judge Lawrence Wheeler told an Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation investigator he used ChatGPT for research and that an order he drafted contained two citations produced by ChatGPT to cases that do not exist. USA Today Network reporting reproduced through Reuters Connect provides the same account, identifies the two fictitious case names, states that the order was issued in a 2025 child-paternity case, and reports that Wheeler later vacated the order after it was challenged.
factual_basis_after: Reuters reports, based on an August 17, 2026 letter from Stephens County District Attorney Jason Hicks to the Oklahoma attorney general's office, that Judge Lawrence Wheeler told an Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation investigator he used ChatGPT for research and that an order he drafted contained two citations produced by ChatGPT to cases that do not exist. USA Today Network reporting reproduced through Reuters Connect provides the same account, identifies the two fictitious case names, states that the order was issued in a 2025 child-paternity case, and reports that Wheeler later vacated the order after it was challenged.
decisive_reasoning: Fictitious AI-produced authority entered an operative paternity-case order. An attorney challenged it and the order was vacated. The meaningful bounded procedural interference and substantive remedy support S3; no lost custody right or ultimate paternity outcome is inferred.
